It is difficult because ambiguity makes the target next-token distribution intrinsically harder for neural networks to represent and fit. More ambiguous distributions require more model capacity, larger embeddings, and more training steps, and they amplify token-sampling noise, which hurts accurate learning of discrete probabilities [1]. One paper calls this a “curse of ambiguity” and reports both theoretical analysis and matching behavior in synthetic and real language-model settings [1].

A complementary controlled study shows the same effect in a minimal ambiguous task: the model first learns the marginal distribution and gets stuck on a loss plateau whose height is exactly set by the ambiguity level, before only later learning the full conditional distribution in a sharp transition [2]. That work also finds gradient noise stabilizes this ambiguous marginal solution, delaying escape to the correct conditional behavior [2].
